## If regression commands are unfamiliar

Use the same object-first workflow throughout Intermediate:

```r
model <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = my_data)
summary(model)
confint(model)
fitted(model)
residuals(model)
plot(model)
```

- `lm()` fits the model specified to the right of `~` and uses the outcome on
  the left.
- `summary()` reports coefficients, their classical tests, model fit, and the
  overall F-test.
- `confint()` reports coefficient confidence intervals.
- `fitted()` and `residuals()` return one value for each analysis row.
- `plot(model)` opens the standard diagnostic plots.

Write the fitted object to a meaningful name and inspect the analysis sample
before interpreting output. R silently omits rows containing missing values in
variables used by `lm()` unless instructed otherwise. The
[Intermediate code sheet](../intermediate/code-sheet.qmd) collects the full
course workflow in one place.

## A five-minute return-to-R check

Run this without copying the displayed answer:

```r
sharks <- read.csv("data/shark_tank_teaching.csv")
nrow(sharks)
mean(sharks$deal_on_show)
median(sharks$description_words)
table(sharks$season)
```

Then explain each output in words. If the code runs but you cannot explain the
quantity, the remaining problem is statistical rather than programming.

## How the figures in this book are made

Every data figure in this textbook carries its own R code --- click
"See the R code for this figure" above any graph to unfold it. Each code
block is self-contained: copy it into a fresh R session in your course
project and it reproduces the figure exactly. Install the plotting packages
once:

```r
install.packages(c("ggplot2", "patchwork"))
```

The figures follow a small set of principles worth stealing for your own
tutorials, reports, and thesis:

- **One message per graph.** The caption states it; everything that does not
  serve it is removed (no boxes, no minor gridlines, no decoration).
- **Counts start at zero, and there is only ever one vertical axis.**
- **Colour is spent, not sprinkled.** One colour carries the data
  (`#009E73`), a second marks contrast or a fitted line (`#D55E00`), grey
  holds context; reference values (means, benchmarks, zero lines) are gold
  dashed lines with the value written next to them. The palette is
  colourblind-safe by construction.
- **Label directly where possible** instead of forcing the reader through a
  legend, and always name axes with their units.
- **PMFs are drawn as stick-and-dot (lollipop) charts**, histograms with
  stated bin widths, model curves as smooth lines with shaded probability
  areas.

If you want to go further --- and for your thesis you will --- three free
references are the course's recommended path: Wickham, Çetinkaya-Rundel &
Grolemund, [*R for Data Science*, Chapter 1](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-visualize)
for ggplot2 itself; Healy,
[*Data Visualization: A Practical Introduction*](https://socviz.co/) for
building good graphs in R end to end; and Wilke,
[*Fundamentals of Data Visualization*](https://clauswilke.com/dataviz/) for
the design principles behind every choice above.
